messages.content:
You are a clinical psychologist writing a psychological case vignette
grounded in Ehlers & Clark's (2000) cognitive model of PTSD.

Write a realistic clinical case vignette for a patient with PTSD.
The vignette should read as a cohesive, flowing portrait — not a structured report.
Weave together who this person is, what happened to them, how they experience their
symptoms day to day, how they cope, and what toll this takes on their life and relationships.


Do not use section headers, numbered points, or clinical labels for symptoms.
Write 200–300 words in third person.
Cover: presenting complaints, trauma background, cognitive distortions, avoidance, and maintaining factors.
Avoid excessive jargon - write for a clinical case conference audience.

Please write a clinical vignette for the following patient presenting with PTSD.
Patient demographics:
- Age: 56
- Gender: Male
- Ethnicity: Oceania
- Relationship Status: Divorced
- Occupation: Detective
- Trauma Type: Physical abuse by caregiver (childhood)
- Pcl5: 62

# Vignette: The Weight of What Was Kept Quiet

---

Reuben is a 56-year-old Māori detective with the kind of face that has learned, over decades, to give nothing away. He carries himself with the particular stillness of a man who has spent thirty years reading other people's silences — interviewing suspects, sitting with grieving families, coaxing truth out of rooms full of fear. He is good at his job. Exceptionally good, his colleagues say. What they do not know is that he learned to read danger long before he ever pinned on a badge.

Reuben grew up in a small coastal town in the North Island, the eldest of five children. His father was a physically powerful man whose moods arrived without warning, the way storms come in off the Tasman — fast, total, and indifferent to whoever happened to be standing in the open. From the time Reuben was around seven until he left home at sixteen, he was beaten regularly. Not chaotically, he explains, but with a kind of cold ritual to it — a belt, a closed fist, the edge of a table. His father never appeared to lose control. That is the part Reuben still cannot reconcile. The deliberateness of it. He learned early to watch for the small signals — the set of his father's jaw, the particular way he placed his beer glass down — and to position himself accordingly. He became, in his own words, *a student of threat*.

He left home, joined the police, and for many years managed to keep what had happened locked in a room he didn't open. He married, had two daughters, and built a life that looked, from the outside, solid and purposeful. But the marriage eroded slowly, then all at once. His ex-wife, Aroha, told him near the end that living with him felt like living with someone who was always waiting for something terrible to happen. He did not argue with her. He knew she was right.

The divorce was finalized eight years ago. Since then, Reuben has lived alone in a flat in Auckland, and it is in that flat, in the hours between midnight and four in the morning, that the past finds him most reliably. He wakes from dreams he cannot always remember but that leave him drenched and rigid, heart hammering against his ribs. Sometimes the dreams are explicit — his father's face, the particular smell of the house, the sound of a belt being pulled through belt loops. Other times there is no clear image, only a sensation of being very small and completely without options.

During the day he functions. He closes cases. He is patient and methodical with victims in ways that younger detectives find remarkable. What they do not see is that he sometimes has to step outside after interviewing a child who has been hurt at home — not to collect himself professionally, but because his hands have begun to shake and his vision has narrowed to a tunnel and his body has decided, without consulting him, that it is 1979 and he is nine years old again.

He avoids his father's side of the family almost entirely. He avoids physical confrontation in ways that require elaborate professional workarounds — he will spend extra hours building a case rather than execute an arrest he could legally make, because the prospect of physical struggle with another man produces in him a shame and a dread he cannot name clearly. He drinks more than he should, though not so much, he tells himself, that it affects his work. He has not been in a relationship since Aroha left.

Reuben is not a man who uses the word *trauma* easily. He is more likely to describe his childhood as *hard* or *not ideal* or, on a candid day, *something I should have dealt with a long time ago*. He came to therapy not because he believed it would help, but because his GP told him his blood pressure was dangerously high and asked whether there was anything he was carrying that he hadn't put down yet.

He sat with that question for a long time before answering.
